strengths: The paper is well-motivated: attaching a lightweight diffusion head to a frozen/learned neural-operator backbone that models a low-rank Karhunen-Loève coefficient space is a sensible and computationally efficient way to add generative UQ capability without abandoning discretization-invariant backbones.

Solid theoretical support: Proposition 2.3 (Wasserstein stability of velocity-matching diffusion training) and Proposition 4.1 (optimality of the operator-encoder as a truncated conditional KL expansion) are carefully proven in the appendix and directly justify the proposed architecture rather than being decorative.

The experimental protocol is reasonably comprehensive, spanning both intrinsically stochastic operator-learning tasks (stochastic Burgers, stochastic Darcy) and deterministic chaotic rollout tasks (KS, Kolmogorov flow), which tests two distinct aspects of the method (aleatoric UQ vs. epistemic/rollout stability).

Baselines are appropriately chosen and cover multiple UQ paradigms (deterministic FNO, MC-dropout, latent-variable PNO, pixel-space diffusion, latent diffusion), enabling a reasonably fair comparison.

The paper reports parameter counts (Tables 8-9) showing DLL is more compact than DM/LDM, supporting the claimed efficiency benefit, and includes qualitative visualizations (mean/std maps, rollout uncertainty bands) that make the calibration claims more interpretable.

The reconstruction-property study (Tables 6-7) is a useful diagnostic that reveals when the input-dependent operator-encoder basis helps (deterministic problems) versus when a plain autoencoder is preferable (stochastic problems), adding nuance rather than uniformly favorable spin.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are frequently marginal and inconsistent: DLL is not the best method on several key metrics (e.g., NRMSEm/NRMSEs in Table 3, NRMSE/CRPS in Table 5 where DM wins), and where DLL does lead (e.g., ED 1.285 vs. DM's 1.355 in Table 2) the margins are small, raising questions about whether the improvements are statistically meaningful given no error bars or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper.

"Architecture agnostic" is a central claim in the abstract/intro, but the method is only ever instantiated and tested with an FNO backbone; no experiments demonstrate the claimed transferability to other operator architectures (DeepONet, transformer-based operators, geometry-aware operators), leaving this claim unverified.

All benchmarks are synthetic, low-dimensional PDE systems (1D Burgers on 256 points, 2D Darcy/KS/Kolmogorov on modest grids); there is no evaluation on larger-scale, higher-resolution, or real-world scientific datasets, which limits the evidence for practical significance and scalability claims made in the discussion (e.g., compatibility with foundation models).

The latent dimension r=64 is fixed across all benchmarks with no ablation, despite it being the key hyperparameter controlling the KL truncation quality vs. diffusion modeling difficulty tradeoff that the theory explicitly discusses.

No wall-clock/sampling-time comparisons are provided despite efficiency being a repeated motivating claim ("substantially reducing computational cost," "efficient sampling"); only static parameter counts are reported, which is a weaker proxy for the claimed inference-time benefits of latent-space diffusion.

The theoretical contributions, while rigorously proven, are largely standard extensions of known results (Wasserstein stability of continuity-equation transport following Kwon et al. 2022 and Ambrosio et al.'s gradient-flow theory; optimal low-rank projection via Karhunen-Loève/PCA-type arguments) rather than fundamentally new theory, and their practical implications (e.g., epistemic uncertainty from diffusion "underfitting") remain largely qualitative/informal rather than empirically validated.

The paper explicitly avoids comparison with function-space diffusion/flow-matching baselines (Lim et al., Kerrigan et al., Shi et al.) that are extensively discussed in the related work, justified only by the fact that benchmarks are on regular grids; this leaves open whether DLL's coefficient-space approach is actually competitive with the more principled function-space alternatives it positions itself against.

Some presented results undercut the paper's core narrative without being fully reconciled: e.g., Table 6/7 show the operator encoder (OE) underperforming a plain autoencoder on the very stochastic benchmarks (Burgers, Darcy) that are the primary motivating use case for DLL, suggesting a tension between the reconstruction-quality argument and the end-to-end distributional results.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: adding principled uncertainty quantification (aleatoric + epistemic) to deterministic neural operator backbones for stochastic PDE learning.

The architecture is conceptually simple and compatible with arbitrary backbones in principle, performing diffusion in a compact, input-adaptive coefficient (truncated KL-type) space rather than in pixel/latent space, which is a reasonable efficiency argument.

The experimental protocol spans both stochastic operator-learning benchmarks (stochastic Burgers, Darcy) and deterministic chaotic rollout benchmarks (KS, Kolmogorov flow), covering distributional metrics (ED, SWD), moment metrics, and rollout calibration metrics (CRPS, SSR).
Substantial theoretical appendix attempting to connect velocity-matching training to Wasserstein-distance guarantees and to formalize the optimality of the rank-r KL-type operator encoder.
Reasonably detailed implementation/appendix documentation (architectures, parameter counts, dataset generation, metrics definitions) supporting some reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical story is inconsistent: DLL is not a clear winner across benchmarks. In Table 3 (Darcy), DM and LDM beat DLL on NRMSEm/NRMSEs; in Table 5 (Kolmogorov rollout), DM clearly outperforms DLL on NRMSE and CRPS, with DLL only marginally best on SSR. This undercuts the central claim that DLL gives a consistently 'strong and consistent trade-off.'

The reconstruction-property ablation (Tables 6-7) actually contradicts the paper's stated advantage of the operator encoder (OE) over a standard autoencoder (AE): AE outperforms OE on the stochastic benchmarks (Burgers, Darcy) and only OE wins on the deterministic ones, yet the text frames OE as generally superior due to input-adaptive basis, which is only partially supported.

The extensive Wasserstein stability theory (Appendix A.1) largely re-derives known continuity-equation stability results (following Kwon et al., 2022) and the link to 'epistemic uncertainty' is asserted qualitatively (via underfitting / Lipschitz-in-c arguments) rather than empirically validated; Proposition 4.1 relies on an unrealistic universal-approximation assumption (Assumption A.11), making it more of a sanity check than a practically meaningful guarantee.

Parameter budgets differ substantially across baselines (Table 8): DM/LDM are 3-4x larger than DLL in 2D, and PNO/FNO/FNO-d share a smaller fixed budget, making it difficult to disentangle whether performance differences stem from the proposed architecture/representation or from capacity/parameterization choices.

No ablation on the key hyperparameter r (latent coefficient dimension, fixed at 64 throughout) or on sensitivity to the number of diffusion steps/samples K, limiting understanding of robustness of the method.

No standard errors, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported for any table, so the small numerical gaps (e.g., ED 1.285 vs 1.355 vs 1.373 in Table 2) cannot be judged as meaningful versus noise.

Novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing ingredients (flow-matching/diffusion, low-rank KL-type coefficient representation, operator-conditioned basis functions) in a relatively direct way; the 'last layer' terminology is somewhat misleading since the method requires training a full separate operator-encoder (basis + coefficient networks) in addition to the diffusion head, rather than a lightweight head on a frozen backbone in the Bayesian-last-layer sense.

Benchmarks are restricted to modest-resolution, standard academic PDEs (1D fields of length 256, 2D fields of 128x128); no evidence is given for scalability to higher-dimensional or more realistic/large-scale operator learning settings despite claims of efficiency gains at 'high resolutions.'

No code/data release or explicit reproducibility statement is mentioned, which combined with the complexity of the pipeline (operator encoder + diffusion head + multiple baselines) raises reproducibility concerns.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential implications of deploying uncertainty estimates from this method in scientific/safety-relevant settings.

strengths: Clean, well-motivated architecture-agnostic idea: attaching a lightweight diffusion head to a neural-operator backbone and performing generation in a compact, input-adaptive truncated Karhunen-Loève coefficient space rather than in pixel/latent space, which is conceptually elegant and computationally efficient.

Solid theoretical backing: a Wasserstein stability bound connecting velocity-matching loss to distributional approximation error (Prop 2.3, with full proofs via continuity-equation stability in App. A.1), and a rigorous characterization of the operator encoder as recovering the optimal rank-r truncated conditional KL subspace (Prop 4.1, App. A.2). These results unify deterministic and stochastic operator learning under one diffusion framework.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning both intrinsically stochastic PDE benchmarks (stochastic Burgers, stochastic Darcy) to test aleatoric UQ, and deterministic chaotic rollout benchmarks (KS, Kolmogorov flow) to test epistemic UQ and long-horizon stability, against a sensible set of baselines (FNO, FNO-dropout, PNO, pixel diffusion, latent diffusion).

Good transparency on compute/parameter budgets (Tables 8-9) showing DLL is substantially more parameter-efficient than pixel-space/latent grid diffusion baselines while remaining competitive in accuracy and calibration (CRPS, SSR, ED, SWD).

Extensive qualitative visualizations (uncertainty bands, spatial standard-deviation maps, error-vs-uncertainty correlation in rollouts) that support the quantitative claims and make the UQ benefits intuitive.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are mixed rather than dominant: DLL is rarely the single best method across all metrics in any table (e.g., PNO wins NRMSEm on Burgers, DM wins NRMSE/CRPS on Kolmogorov rollout, LDM slightly beats DLL on SWD for Darcy), and the paper's framing as a 'strong and consistent trade-off' slightly overstates what the numbers show.

Generality claims are not empirically substantiated: the abstract/intro advertise DLL as 'architecture agnostic' and preserving 'geometry handling,' but all experiments use only the FNO backbone on regular grids; no results with DeepONet, transformer-based, or irregular-geometry operators are shown to support this claim.

The comparison between the operator encoder (OE) and a standard autoencoder (Tables 6-7) is inconclusive and somewhat undercuts the paper's motivation for OE: AE reconstructs better on stochastic benchmarks while OE is better only on deterministic ones, despite much higher compression ratios for OE, and no downstream-task ablation isolates the encoder's actual contribution to UQ quality versus the diffusion head itself.

No ablation on the key hyperparameter r (latent/coefficient dimension, fixed at 64 throughout) or on diffusion training details (number of steps T=10, sampling budget K=32), leaving sensitivity and robustness of the method unclear.
No indication of multiple random seeds, variance, or statistical significance for the reported metrics, limiting confidence in the (often small) margins between competing methods.

The theoretical contributions, while rigorous, are largely adaptations of existing Wasserstein-stability results for flow/diffusion models (building on Kwon et al. 2022) rather than fundamentally new insight specific to operator learning; their practical necessity for justifying the proposed architecture (versus being a nice-to-have formalism) is not strongly demonstrated.
No explicit wall-clock/sampling-time comparison is reported despite efficiency being a stated selling point; only parameter counts are given.

The limitations and ethical considerations discussion is essentially absent (boilerplate impact statement), despite the method having clear limitations (fixed backbone, regular grids, no uncertainty calibration guarantees) that merit explicit discussion.

strengths: Well-motivated architectural idea: attaching a conditional diffusion/flow-matching head to a neural operator backbone in a compact, input-dependent coefficient space (inspired by KL expansions) rather than in pixel or generic latent space, which plausibly improves sampling efficiency while retaining discretization invariance.

Reasonably rigorous theoretical support: Proposition 2.3/A.2 gives a Wasserstein stability bound linking the velocity-matching loss to distributional error, and Proposition 4.1/A.7-A.9 characterizes the operator encoder's optimal solution as a conditional (uncentered) Karhunen-Loeve subspace, giving a principled interpretation of the coefficient representation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two stochastic PDE benchmarks (Burgers, Darcy) and two deterministic chaotic rollout benchmarks (KS, Kolmogorov flow), with a sensible set of baselines spanning deterministic, dropout-based, Bayesian-flavored (PNO), pixel-space diffusion, and latent diffusion models.

Extensive ablations on latent rank, number of function evaluations (NFE), training dataset size, and backbone compatibility (DeepONet on an inverse problem), which add useful practical guidance and partially support robustness of the method.

Clear and honest reporting of mixed results (e.g., autoencoder sometimes outperforming the operator encoder in raw reconstruction, DM sometimes outperforming DLL on Kolmogorov rollout), together with qualitative visualizations (mean/std maps, sample trajectories) that substantiate the quantitative claims.
Reasonably detailed appendix with dataset generation, architecture, and metric definitions supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Empirical results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: DLL is not best on several key metrics (e.g., NRMSEm/NRMSEs on stochastic Darcy, NRMSE/CRPS on Kolmogorov flow rollout where pixel-space DM wins), so the abstract's characterization of 'strong distributional fidelity' somewhat overstates the consistency of the gains.

The theoretical results, while nicely presented, rely on fairly strong/idealized assumptions (e.g., Assumption A.11 universal approximation for the operator encoder) that do not hold for the actual finite-capacity FNO/MLP architectures used in experiments, limiting the practical bite of Propositions 2.3 and 4.1 beyond providing qualitative intuition.

The core algorithmic idea (diffusion/flow matching over coefficients w.r.t. a learned basis) is conceptually incremental relative to existing spectral diffusion, latent diffusion, and function-space diffusion literature already cited in the paper; the main novelty is the input-dependent (rather than fixed) basis, which is a modest but real contribution.

Benchmarks are relatively small scale (1D length-256 fields, 2D 128x128 grids, training sets of a few thousand to ten thousand samples), and no larger-scale, higher-resolution, or more realistic scientific dataset is tested, so claims about a 'practical route to uncertainty aware neural operators' are not yet strongly substantiated at scale.

No error bars or repeated-run statistics are reported for any table, making it hard to assess whether the reported differences between DLL and close baselines (e.g., PNO, DM) are statistically meaningful.

The rank ablation shows non-monotone (sometimes worsening) downstream distributional/rollout metrics as reconstruction fidelity improves with larger r, an interesting but unexplained inconsistency that is not analyzed in depth.

Comparison to genuinely Bayesian neural operator baselines (e.g., variational or ensemble-based approaches referenced in related work) is absent; only MC dropout is used as an epistemic-uncertainty baseline, which is a weak proxy and may understate the difficulty of the comparison landscape.

strengths: The paper proposes a clean, modular architectural idea: attaching a conditional diffusion/flow-matching head to a neural operator backbone that operates in a compact, input-dependent coefficient space rather than pixel or generic-autoencoder latent space.

Reasonably thorough theoretical framing connecting velocity-matching training to Wasserstein endpoint error (Prop 2.3/A.2) and characterizing the optimal rank-r operator encoder as a conditional (uncentered) Karhunen-Loeve subspace (Prop 4.1/A.9), which gives the design some formal grounding.

Broad experimental coverage spanning both aleatoric (stochastic Burgers, stochastic Darcy) and epistemic/rollout (KS, Kolmogorov flow) settings, with multiple baselines (FNO, FNO-dropout, PNO, pixel DM, LDM) and several ablations (rank, NFE, dataset size, DeepONet backbone).
Clear pipeline figures and a reasonably well-organized presentation of the method and its relation to prior UQ/generative-operator literature.
weaknesses: The paper's own ablation (Tables 6–7) shows the proposed operator encoder actually reconstructs worse than a plain autoencoder in 3 of 4 benchmarks (Burgers, Darcy, Kolmogorov), and only wins on KS. This directly undercuts the central motivating claim that an input-dependent KL-type basis is a better representation for coefficient-space diffusion, and the paper's post-hoc rationalization ('operator conditioned features capture dominant low-dimensional structure... despite higher compression') is not convincingly supported.

Empirical improvements from DLL are marginal and inconsistent across benchmarks: it is not uniformly best (e.g., on stochastic Darcy DLL is best on ED but worse than PNO/DM on NRMSEm/NRMSEs; on Kolmogorov-flow rollout, pixel-space DM clearly beats DLL on NRMSE and CRPS). This weakens the significance claim that 'diffusion modeling in learned coefficient spaces offers a practical route to uncertainty-aware neural operators.'

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere in the main tables or ablations, despite many reported differences between methods being small (e.g., third-decimal differences in SWD/NRMSE), making it hard to assess whether the claimed improvements are real or noise.

The rank ablation (Table 10–11) shows non-monotonic and sometimes counter-intuitive behavior (e.g., larger rank improving reconstruction but not distributional metrics), which is not carefully explained and raises concerns about the stability/robustness of the coefficient-space diffusion training.

Conceptually, the contribution is incremental relative to existing latent-diffusion-for-PDEs and spectral/KL-basis diffusion work already cited by the authors (e.g., Phillips et al. 2022, Rozet et al. 2025); the main novelty is swapping a generic autoencoder latent for an operator-conditioned coefficient basis, which the paper's own reconstruction results suggest is not clearly superior.

The DeepONet compatibility experiment (Table 15) is on a narrow, low-dimensional inverse problem and does not show a clear win for DLL (DeepONet-Dropout has the best NRMSE), so it provides weak evidence for backbone-agnostic generality.

The theoretical propositions, while nice to include, rely on fairly strong/idealized assumptions (e.g., universal approximation for the operator encoder, Lipschitz velocity fields) that are not empirically verified, and the core stability result (Prop 2.3) is a fairly standard application of known continuity-equation stability estimates rather than a novel theoretical contribution.

The impact statement is generic boilerplate and does not engage with any limitations specific to deploying probabilistic PDE surrogates (e.g., miscalibration risk in safety-critical simulation contexts), which is a missed opportunity given the paper's UQ focus.

Uncertainty calibration is only assessed via SSR in the rollout tasks; no calibration/coverage metric is reported for the stochastic distributional benchmarks despite these being the primary use case for aleatoric UQ.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: adding calibrated uncertainty quantification to neural operators while preserving discretization invariance.

The proposed low-rank coefficient-space parameterization is theoretically well-motivated: Proposition 4.1 rigorously shows that the reconstruction loss recovers an input-conditional (uncentered) Karhunen-Loève-type optimal rank-r subspace, and Proposition 2.3/Appendix A.1 provides a clean Wasserstein stability bound connecting velocity matching loss to distributional error, unifying deterministic and stochastic operator learning under one framework.

Experimental coverage is broad and includes both stochastic PDE benchmarks (Burgers, Darcy) and deterministic chaotic rollout benchmarks (KS, Kolmogorov flow), evaluated against a reasonably comprehensive set of baselines (FNO, MC-dropout FNO, PNO, pixel-space diffusion, latent diffusion).

Extensive and informative ablations are provided (coefficient rank, NFE, training set size, DeepONet backbone compatibility), which strengthen confidence in the design choices and demonstrate modularity beyond the FNO backbone.

The coefficient-space approach offers a clear practical efficiency advantage over pixel-space/latent diffusion (fewer parameters, fewer NFEs needed) while remaining competitive in distributional fidelity metrics.
Qualitative visualizations (mean/std maps, rollout uncertainty bands, error-vs-uncertainty correlation) support the claim that DLL uncertainty estimates track meaningful spatial structure in errors.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are often small and inconsistent across benchmarks/metrics: DM outperforms DLL on Kolmogorov flow NRMSE/CRPS, and results are not accompanied by error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust rather than noise, especially given modest test set sizes (32 test inputs).

The operator encoder (OE) does not consistently outperform a plain autoencoder (AE): Tables 6-7 show OE is worse than AE on the stochastic benchmarks (Burgers, Darcy) despite the paper's framing of KL-adapted bases as advantageous; this weakens the core motivating claim for using an input-dependent basis in the stochastic setting.

The theoretical contributions, while correct and clearly presented, are relatively standard applications of known results (stability of the continuity/transport equation, Eckart–Young-type optimal low-rank projection) rather than fundamentally new theory; their practical implications for guiding architecture/hyperparameter choices are somewhat limited, as shown by the ablations where reconstruction error improvements do not translate monotonically into better distributional metrics.

The heuristic claim that non-zero diffusion loss L_V(c) can serve as a qualitative epistemic uncertainty indicator (Section 3.3) is not empirically validated with a dedicated experiment (e.g., correlating L_V with actual epistemic error across varying data regimes), leaving this interpretive claim under-supported.

The two-stage training pipeline (separately trained, frozen operator encoder followed by diffusion training in coefficient space) adds complexity and potential suboptimality (encoder is not jointly optimized with the generative objective), which is not discussed as a limitation or ablated against end-to-end alternatives.
Computational cost/wall-clock comparisons (training and inference time) are not directly reported, only parameter counts, limiting a full assessment of the claimed efficiency advantage.

The paper's conclusion that DLL's performance ceiling depends on backbone quality (as observed for Kolmogorov flow) somewhat limits the generality of the claimed contribution, since the paper does not explore stronger operator backbones for this harder benchmark.
